title: Select All Columns from a Table
story: You have just joined TechCorp as a Data Analyst. The HR Operations Team needs a complete snapshot of all employee records currently stored in the company database to conduct an end-of-quarter headcount audit. Your task is to extract every record and every attribute from the employees table to ensure no team member is omitted from the audit report.
objective: Write an SQL query to retrieve all columns and all rows from the employees table.
starter_code:
-- Problem #Basics-001: Select all columns from a table
-- Write your SQL query below
expected_output:
employee_id | first_name | last_name | email | phone_number | hire_date | job_title | salary | manager_id | department_id | age | city | gender | state
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1 | John | Doe | john.doe@email.com | 555-0101 | 2020-01-15 | Software Engineer | 85000.0 | NULL | 101 | 28 | New York | Male | NY
2 | Jane | Smith | jane.smith@email.com | 555-0102 | 2019-03-22 | Engineering Manager | 120000.0 | NULL | 101 | 35 | New York | Female | NY
3 | Bob | Johnson | bob.j@email.com | 555-0103 | 2021-06-01 | Sales Exec | 60000.0 | 2 | 102 | 32 | Chicago | Male | IL
4 | Alice | Williams | alice.w@email.com | 555-0104 | 2018-11-12 | Sales Director | 110000.0 | NULL | 102 | 40 | Chicago | Female | IL
5 | Charlie | Brown | charlie.b@email.com | 555-0105 | 2022-02-10 | Marketing Specialist | 55000.0 | 4 | 103 | 25 | San Francisco | Male | CA
6 | Diana | Prince | diana.p@email.com | 555-0106 | 2017-08-05 | HR Lead | 75000.0 | NULL | 104 | 38 | Boston | Female | MA
7 | Eva | Green | eva.g@email.com | 555-0107 | 2023-01-01 | Software Engineer | 90000.0 | 2 | 101 | 26 | New York | Female | NY
8 | Frank | Miller | frank.m@email.com | 555-0108 | 2020-09-15 | Financial Analyst | 70000.0 | NULL | 105 | 30 | New York | Male | NY
hints: SELECT tells the database that you want to retrieve data.
* (asterisk) means all columns.
FROM tells SQL where the data is stored (employees table).

test_cases.expected: employee_id | first_name | last_name | email | phone_number | hire_date | job_title | salary | manager_id | department_id | age | city | gender | state
test_cases.description: Verify all 14 columns from employees table

explanation:
SELECT *
FROM table_name;

🔍 Query Breakdown
Line 1: SELECT *
- SELECT tells the database that you want to retrieve data.
- * (asterisk) means all columns.
Instead of writing all columns explicitly, you can simply write SELECT * because * automatically selects every column.

Line 2: FROM table_name;
FROM tells SQL where the data is stored. Here, table_name is the table name.

⚙️ SQL Execution Order:
Step 1: FROM table_name (Locate the specified table)
Step 2: SELECT * (Retrieve every column from every row)

Execution Flow:
table_name ──► Read every row ──► Read every column ──► Display result

🚀 Alternative Solutions:
Method 1 (Recommended):
```sql
SELECT *
FROM table_name;
```

Method 2 (Explicit Column Names):
```sql
SELECT column1, column2, column3
FROM table_name;
```

⚡ Performance Notes:
SELECT * retrieves all columns, good for learning/debugging. In production, requesting only needed columns saves memory and bandwidth.

title: Select Specific Columns
story: The Internal Communications & Security team is preparing an updated employee directory for the company intranet. For privacy and performance reasons, they strictly request only public fields (employee ID, first name, last name, job title, and salary) without exposing internal infrastructure flags or manager IDs.
objective: Write an SQL query to display only the following columns from the employees table: employee_id, first_name, last_name, job_title, salary.
starter_code:
-- Problem #Basics-002: Select Specific Columns
-- Write your SQL query below
expected_output:
employee_id | first_name | last_name | job_title | salary
---------------------------------------------------------------
1 | John | Doe | Software Engineer | 85000.0
2 | Jane | Smith | Engineering Manager | 120000.0
3 | Bob | Johnson | Sales Exec | 60000.0
4 | Alice | Williams | Sales Director | 110000.0
5 | Charlie | Brown | Marketing Specialist | 55000.0
6 | Diana | Prince | HR Lead | 75000.0
7 | Eva | Green | Software Engineer | 90000.0
8 | Frank | Miller | Financial Analyst | 70000.0
hints: SELECT tells the database which columns to retrieve.
Separate column names with commas: employee_id, first_name, last_name, job_title, salary.
FROM employees specifies the source table.

test_cases.expected: employee_id | first_name | last_name | job_title | salary
test_cases.description: Verify 5 selected columns from employees table

explanation:
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, job_title, salary
FROM employees;

🔍 Query Breakdown
Line 1: SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, job_title, salary
- SELECT tells SQL that you want to retrieve data.
- Instead of using SELECT *, we select only five specific columns:
  - employee_id: Unique ID of the employee
  - first_name: Employee's first name
  - last_name: Employee's last name
  - job_title: Employee's designation
  - salary: Employee's salary

Line 2: FROM employees;
FROM tells SQL where to retrieve the data. Here, SQL looks inside the employees table.

⚙️ SQL Execution Order:
Step 1: FROM employees (Locate the employees table)
Step 2: SELECT columns (Retrieve only the specified columns)

Execution Flow:
employees table ──► Read every row ──► Pick only specified columns ──► Display Result

🚀 Alternative Solutions:
Method 1 (Recommended):
```sql
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, job_title, salary FROM employees;
```

Method 2 (Select All Columns):
```sql
SELECT * FROM employees;
```

Method 2 also includes the required columns, but it retrieves unnecessary data and is not recommended when you only need a few columns.

⚡ Performance Notes:
Method 1 reads only required columns, making it faster and preferred in production. Method 2 retrieves unnecessary columns, increasing memory and network usage.

title: Use Multiple Conditions with AND
story: The Finance & HR Operations Team is planning senior tier bonus packages specifically for high-earning engineering team members. To qualify, an employee must work in Department 101 AND earn a salary greater than $60,000. Your task is to query the database and retrieve records for employees who meet both strict criteria.

starter_code:
-- Problem #Basics-004: Use Multiple Conditions with AND
-- Write your SQL query below
expected_output:
employee_id | first_name | last_name | email | phone_number | hire_date | job_title | salary | manager_id | department_id | age | city | gender | state
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1 | John | Doe | john.doe@email.com | 555-0101 | 2020-01-15 | Software Engineer | 85000.0 | NULL | 101 | 28 | New York | Male | NY
2 | Jane | Smith | jane.smith@email.com | 555-0102 | 2019-03-22 | Engineering Manager | 120000.0 | NULL | 101 | 35 | New York | Female | NY
7 | Eva | Green | eva.g@email.com | 555-0107 | 2023-01-01 | Software Engineer | 90000.0 | 2 | 101 | 26 | New York | Female | NY
hints: SELECT * retrieves all columns from the table.
FROM employees specifies the target table.
WHERE department_id = 101 AND salary > 60000 combines both required conditions.

test_cases.expected: department_id = 101 AND salary > 60000
test_cases.description: Verify filtered rows where department_id is 101 and salary is > 60000

explanation:
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 101
AND salary > 60000;

🔍 Query Breakdown
Line 1: SELECT *
- SELECT tells SQL to retrieve data.
- * returns all columns.

Line 2: FROM employees
- FROM specifies the source table.

Line 3-4: WHERE department_id = 101 AND salary > 60000;
- WHERE filters rows based on logical conditions.
- AND requires BOTH conditions to evaluate to TRUE for a row to be included.

⚙️ SQL Execution Order:
Step 1: FROM employees (Locate target table)
Step 2: Read every row
Step 3: Evaluate department_id = 101
Step 4: Evaluate salary > 60000
Step 5: SELECT * (Return matching rows where both conditions are TRUE)

Execution Flow:
employees ──► Read every row ──► Check department_id = 101 ──► Check salary > 60000 ──► Keep if BOTH TRUE ──► Display result

🚀 Alternative Solutions:
Method 1 (Recommended):
```sql
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 101
AND salary > 60000;
```

Method 2 (Specific Columns):
```sql
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 101
AND salary > 60000;
```

⚡ Performance Notes:
Using AND allows SQL engines to leverage composite indexes or evaluate highly selective filters first, reducing intermediate dataset size and boosting query execution speed.

Line 1: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS total_employees
- Projects the grouping key department_id and aliased count.

Line 2: FROM employees
- Reads the employees table.

Line 3: GROUP BY department_id
- Partitions employees into departmental groups.

Line 4: HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
- Filters the summarized groups, retaining only those where the calculated group count exceeds 2.

⚙️ SQL Execution Order:
Step 1: FROM employees ── Read table
Step 2: GROUP BY department_id ── Create groups
Step 3: COUNT(*) ── Calculate count for every group
Step 4: HAVING COUNT(*) > 2 ── Discard groups that do not satisfy condition
Step 5: Display remaining groups
